###### Abstract

Language models are increasingly used for moral decision-making across
diverse linguistic and cultural contexts, yet existing work overlooks
multilinguality on three aspects: 1) multilingual evaluation benchmarks
use direct translation, failing to adapt culture-specific items; 2)
inference-time methods for moral reasoning rely on static,
English-centric scaffolds and lack grounding in moral theory; 3)
training methods for moral decision-making typically require expensive
supervision from stronger models or human annotators. We address these
gaps with three contributions. First, we introduce MCLASH, a
multilingual moral decision-making benchmark to capture culturally
situated moral intuitions and social norms across languages. Second, we
propose MET (Multilingual Ethics with Theory-grounded reasoning), a
two-step prompting method built on expert-curated, theory-based grounds
drawn from psychology and philosophy: the model first selects situation-
and culture-specific grounds, then reasons over them in the native
language of the user. Third, we introduce MET-D (MET-Distillation),
which enhances the second step through a self-distillation training
stage that requires no external supervision. MET-D improves macro-F1
over the base model on all three models of different sizes and families
(Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma3-4B), by an average of 3.71 points on MCLASH
and 4.23 on MMoralExceptQA, with a peak MCLASH gain of 12.94 points for
Malay on Qwen3-8B. We further reveal that MET-D increases
native-language reasoning by 62.13 points on average, and that
beneficial grounds differ systematically across cultures. Together,
these contributions open the path for culture-aligned, theory-grounded
multilingual moral reasoning.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2607.11736v1/dimension_prompt_examples_new.png)

Figure 1: Example ground selection in different languages: Grounds are
organized into dimensions and paired with descriptions. For the same
situation, the selected grounds vary by language: in English,
First-principles reasoning reflects the Western rationalism, whereas in
Korean, Contractarianism reflects Confucian values.

Language models are increasingly deployed in moral decision-making
across high-stakes domains such as law ([Xiao et al., 2021](#bib.bib33);
[Nguyen, 2023](#bib.bib32)) and healthcare ([Singhal et al.,
2023](#bib.bib31); [Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib30)), where users span
diverse cultural backgrounds. Effective deployment in such settings
requires that models reason within the linguistic and cultural context
of the user, accounting for the local value systems that shape a sound
moral judgment. However, culturally aligned moral decision-making
remains overlooked in both evaluation and methods.

Evaluation: direct translation strips cultural context from moral
dilemmas. Existing multilingual moral benchmarks directly translate
English scenarios ([Kumar and Jurgens, 2025](#bib.bib34); [Farid et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)) without adapting culture-specific items ([Newmark,
1988](#bib.bib37)) such as named entities, institutions, currencies, and
customs. When directly translated into Korean or Hindi, a U.S. scenario
set during “Thanksgiving” or at a “Wendy’s” can import improper Western
cultural context into account. We address this with MCLASH, a
multilingual moral decision-making benchmark built by culturally
adapting CLASH ([Lee et al., 2025](#bib.bib3))—a corpus of long-form
high-stakes scenarios paired with character descriptions—into five
additional languages (Chinese, Hindi, Korean, Malay, Spanish).
Adaptation is performed by Qwen3-32B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib38))
and then inspected by native speakers, yielding 1,852 situations and
9,260 character descriptions.

Method (inference): existing scaffolds lack theory grounding, culture-
and situation-specific adaptation, and multilingual support. Beyond
producing the correct decision, the reasoning that justifies it must be
reliable and understandable for users to audit ([Gilpin et al.,
2018](#bib.bib36); [Besold and Uckelman, 2018](#bib.bib35)). Theoretical
grounding can improve reasoning quality in moral decision-making
([Chakraborty et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)), yet most existing methods do
not engage with moral theories such as deontology or care ethics ([Jin
et al., 2022](#bib.bib14); [AlKhamissi et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)). Even
the theory-grounded work ([Chakraborty et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)) covers
only a narrow set of theories and applies them without cultural or
situational adaptation. Research on moral reasoning is also largely
English-only; methods are developed and evaluated on English benchmarks
([Chiu et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)), and multilingual reasoning techniques
borrowed from culture-agnostic tasks assume a language-invariant
reasoning structure ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Zhu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib26); [She et al., 2024](#bib.bib27); [Zhao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib22); [Yoon et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)), which does not hold
when moral frameworks vary by culture.

We address these gaps with MET (Multilingual Ethics with Theory-grounded
reasoning), a two-step prompting method in which the model first selects
the grounds most relevant to the given situation, then uses them to
produce a grounded reasoning chain in the native language of the user
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")).
The full, multilingual set of grounds from which the model selects is
developed by the authors including a domain expert¹¹ 1 One of the
authors, Peter Railton, is a professor of ethics, value theory, and
moral psychology., drawing on psychology and philosophy literature, and
organized into six high-level dimensions (e.g., Value Systems, Conflict
Handling Strategies).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: Sparse theory-guided reasoning behavior in the base model. On
26-scug (English), the base explicitly mentions only two of its ten
grounds, Institution-Based and Responsibility-Based, both weighing the
duty to uphold ethics standards, and collapses to a definitive yes
(punish) rather than the correct ambiguous, under-weighting the
character’s equal commitment to forgiving an honest miscommunication.

Method (training): training the model to ground its reasoning in moral
theory suffers from a lack of verifiable signals. Prompting alone is
insufficient: even when the model selects relevant grounds, the
reasoning chain frequently engages with only a few
(Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")),
leaving the rest unaddressed and producing shallow, one-sided judgments.
However, training the model to substantively engage with the grounds is
hard because moral decision-making is subjective and generally lacks the
verifiable ground truth that enables rejection sampling ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib89); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib90)); existing methods
therefore rely on distillation from stronger models or extensive human
involvement ([Tennant et al., 2025](#bib.bib91); [An and Du,
2026](#bib.bib92); [Feng et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)). We sidestep this by
constructing a synthetic dataset that follows the structure of CLASH:
each dilemma is paired with a character whose value priorities make the
correct decision automatically verifiable. MET-D (MET-Distillation) then
applies rejection-sampling self-distillation on this dataset, using
correct decisions as a proxy for substantive engagement with the
grounds.

On MCLASH, MET-D improves the average F1 score by 3.71 points over the
base model across three models spanning different sizes and families
(Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma3-4B), with the largest single gain of
12.94 points for Malay on Qwen3-8B. These improvements generalize to
other datasets, reaching 4.23 points on average for MMoralExceptQA([Jin
et al., 2022](#bib.bib14)) and 3.53 points for MoCa([Nie et al.,
2023](#bib.bib10)) on Qwen3-4B. Beyond performance, MET-D increases
native-language reasoning by 62.13 percentage points on Qwen3-4B, making
the reasoning more legible for non-English speakers. We further find
that the most beneficial grounds for each culture align with its actual
cultural characteristics, and that cross-lingual transfer follows
linguistic typology rather than cultural similarity.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  MCLASH, a multilingual moral decision-making benchmark of 1,852
  long-form scenarios across six languages, constructed by cultural
  adaptation rather than direct translation.
- •
  Expert-curated theoretical grounds for moral reasoning, organized into
  six high-level dimensions and translated into all six languages.
- •
  MET, a two-step prompting method that employs situation- and
  culture-specific grounds, and MET-D, which extends MET with a
  self-distillation training stage that requires no external
  supervision.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Moral Decision-Making Datasets

Most previous work in moral decision-making either probes the
preferences of the models rather than providing an answer, which makes
it hard to assess their actual decision-making ability ([Chiu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib2); [Samway et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Wu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib7); [Wu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib8)), or does not consider
multilinguality, thereby overlooking the cultural differences in making
judgments ([Lee et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Scherrer et al.,
2024](#bib.bib9); [Nie et al., 2023](#bib.bib10)). Some recent studies
incorporate multilinguality, but their scenarios are either short, fewer
than three sentences, which limits their narrative complexity ([Farid et
al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Pistilli et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)), or rely on
direct translation ([Farid et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Jin et
al.,](#bib.bib5) ) without accounting for cultural adaptation. We
address these gaps by introducing a new multilingual dataset, MCLASH,
that includes culturally-adapted long scenarios.

### 2.2 Inference-Time Methods for Moral Decision-Making

Most inference-time methods for moral decision-making rely on structured
prompting ([AlKhamissi et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Jin et al.,
2022](#bib.bib14); [Chakraborty et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)), but apply
the same framework to every dilemma. This approach is insufficient,
since the appropriate moral framework varies with the context of each
dilemma ([Fletcher, 1966](#bib.bib16); [Dancy, 2004](#bib.bib17)). In
contrast, MoReBench ([Chiu et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)) addresses
per-instance adaptation through rubrics for evaluating moral reasoning.
While the rubrics can be adapted as inference-time guidance, they are
coarse, atheoretical, English-only, and labor-intensive to construct.
Closest to our approach, [Chakraborty et al. (2025)](#bib.bib12) shows
that theoretical scaffolds improve reasoning quality, but uses a narrow,
static, and English-only set of theories. MET combines theory grounding
with multilingual support and per-instance, per-language adaptation,
enabling culture-aligned reasoning in the native language of the end
user.

### 2.3 Multilingual Training for Moral Decision-Making

Methods developed for conventional reasoning domains such as math and
code treat non-English reasoning as a translation of English reasoning,
which assumes the same reasoning structure across languages. Common
techniques include aligning non-English representations toward the
English subspace ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib23)), optimizing for
similarity between non-English and English reasoning chains ([She et
al., 2024](#bib.bib27)), and bridging multilingual encoders with
English-trained reasoners that apply English reasoning patterns to
inputs in any language ([Zhao et al., 2025](#bib.bib22); [Yoon et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)). These approaches fail in moral decision-making,
where different cultures apply different moral frameworks reflecting
their distinct values ([Hwang et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Myung et al.,
2024](#bib.bib25)).

Existing training methods for moral reasoning rely on heavy external
supervision via hand-crafted rewards ([Tennant et al.,
2025](#bib.bib91)) or stronger models ([An and Du, 2026](#bib.bib92)),
and operate only in English. In the multilingual space, prior work is
largely evaluation-focused ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib93); [Kumar
and Jurgens, 2025](#bib.bib34); [Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib94)), and
training methods target cultural commonsense rather than reasoning
through moral dilemmas where values conflict, using cultural surveys
([Li et al., 2024a](#bib.bib19)), multi-agent debates ([Li et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib20)), fine-grained critique ([Feng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib18)), or culture-aware self-improvement ([Xu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib29)). MET-D directly targets moral decision-making and
self-supervises via the character-paired structure of CLASH.

## 3 Construction of MCLASH

CLASH ([Lee et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) consists of 345 high-stakes
situations paired with 3,795 character descriptions, and tasks models
with making a decision from the perspective of the character. We adapt
the original English situations into five languages (Chinese, Hindi,
Korean, Malay, and Spanish) and their corresponding cultures²² 2
Cultural boundaries are inherently dynamic and uncertain ([Delanoy,
2020](#bib.bib95)), and can be defined by various criteria such as
religion, geography, or language. Following common practice in
cross-cultural NLP ([Naous et al., 2024](#bib.bib21); [Maji et al.,
2025](#bib.bib96); [Onohara et al., 2025](#bib.bib97)), we use language
as a proxy for culture and consider all regions where each language is
spoken. using Qwen3-32B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)), selected for
its adaptation quality
(Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Selection of the model for adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")).
Next, native speakers review and modify the narratives with a rigorous
checklist (Figure
[11](#A1.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ A.2 Details of Adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning"))
to ensure cultural relevance. When a situation seems entirely irrelevant
to a given culture, we discuss with the inspectors and discard it if
necessary. We then adapt the character descriptions based on the adapted
situations, followed by an additional round of human inspection.

Importantly, this process does not involve direct translation, a
limitation of previous work. Instead, we carefully adapt each instance
to preserve culturally specific nuances. For example, instead of
directly translating “Amazon”, the American big-tech company, we
instruct the inspectors to adapt it to other big-tech companies in their
culture, such as “Naver” and “Kakao” in Korea. We refer to the resulting
dataset as MCLASH, which consists of 1,852 situations and 9,260
character descriptions. Details of adaptation, human inspection, and
data statistics are presented in Appendices
[A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Details of Adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
and
[A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").

## 4 Method

In
§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Theoretical Grounds ‣ 4 Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning"),
we describe how we curate the theoretical grounds. We then present 1)
MET, our two-step prompting method of selecting and applying the
grounds, and 2) MET-D, which constructs a training dataset and adds a
rejection-sampling distillation stage on top of MET in
§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Guiding Reasoning using Grounds ‣ 4 Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").

### 4.1 Theoretical Grounds

In collaboration with a domain expert, we curate a global set of
theoretical grounds, translated into all six languages, for the model to
select from. A total of 37 grounds are organized into six dimensions,
each paired with a description that helps the model understand the
ground and select the most relevant ones. This uniform structure makes
the set easy to extend: a new ground can be added simply by specifying
its dimension and description without changing the selection process.
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
shows an example of these grounds and their dimensions.

We explain each dimension below, with the full list of grounds and
descriptions provided in Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Details of Grounds and Prompts ‣ Appendix B Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").
The Normative Authority dimension ([Railton, 1986](#bib.bib39); [Wood,
2008](#bib.bib40); [Reus-Smit and others, 2005](#bib.bib41), e.g.,)
establishes the foundational premises for the reasoning process, while
Value Systems ([Graham et al., 2013](#bib.bib53); [Schwartz,
2012](#bib.bib54), e.g.,) identify the values that should be taken into
account. Ethical Theories ([Alexander and Moore, 2007](#bib.bib57);
[Mill, 2016](#bib.bib58), e.g.,) provide the normative structure guiding
the reasoning, and Cognitive Reasoning Strategies ([Wei et al.,
2022](#bib.bib82); [Freeman, 2010](#bib.bib83), e.g.,) outline its
underlying cognitive structure. Finally, Conflict Handling Strategies
([Dancy, 2001](#bib.bib65); [Musschenga, 2005](#bib.bib66), e.g.,) and
Moral Uncertainty ([Ess, 2006](#bib.bib63); [MacAskill et al.,
2020](#bib.bib77), e.g.,) address approaches for navigating dilemmas and
managing uncertainty in moral decision-making.

### 4.2 Guiding Reasoning using Grounds

Figure 3: Method: In MET, the model first selects situation- and
language-specific grounds, then reasons based on them. MET-D extends
this by adding a self-distillation training stage to improve
theory-guided reasoning. The training dataset for MET-D is synthetically
generated using Qwen3-32B, following a
situation-and-character-description structure where ground-truth labels
are automatically derivable without manual annotation.

MET. Given a situation, MET guides the target model in two steps (Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Guiding Reasoning using Grounds ‣ 4 Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")): 1)
Ground Selection: The model is prompted with the dimensions, grounds,
and descriptions, and asked to select the grounds most relevant to the
given situation, forming an instance-specific framework. 2)
Theory-Guided Reasoning: Given the selected grounds and the situation,
the model outputs the reasoning and the answer. The prompts are
presented in Figures
[14](#A2.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ B.1 Details of Grounds and Prompts ‣ Appendix B Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
to
[16](#A2.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ B.1 Details of Grounds and Prompts ‣ Appendix B Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").

MET-D. Analysis of the initial results reveals that in the second step,
models often engage with only a subset of the grounds they select,
leaving the rest unaddressed, thus producing shallow reasoning (Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")).
To enhance the utilization of the selected grounds in theory-guided
reasoning, we introduce additional training using a synthetic dataset
that follows the structure of CLASH. We refer to this training
procedure, along with the subsequent MET prompting, as MET-D
(MET-Distillation). Moral dilemmas typically require human annotation
for ground-truth answers, especially “ambiguous” ones. CLASH circumvents
this by pairing each situation with well-defined character descriptions
whose value priorities determine the ground-truth decision, eliminating
the need for human supervision. CLASH also captures moral ambivalence
through ternary labels (yes/no/ambiguous) rather than clear-cut yes/no.

The training dataset is constructed as follows. We first derive a
comprehensive cultural value set by extracting relevant values from the
WVS questionnaire ([WVS, 2023](#bib.bib45); [Sheetal et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46)) using multiple models (Qwen3-32B and GPT-oss-120B),
then taking the union of the resulting value sets, with the prompt used
for extraction presented in Figure
[17](#A2.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ B.2 Prompts Used for Generating the Training Dataset ‣ Appendix B Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").
For each dilemma, we randomly sample three values from the constructed
value set per side and prompt Qwen3-32B to generate a corresponding
scenario. We then follow the prompts used in CLASH to generate five
character descriptions per scenario, each associated with a yes, no, or
ambiguous ground-truth decision. We generate 500 scenarios and 2,500
character descriptions per language. To ensure topic diversity, each
dilemma is additionally conditioned on one of six high-stakes topics
(Government, Medical, Business, Journalism, Education, and Technology),
equally distributed across generated scenarios.

Using this dataset, we prompt the target model $`M`$ to select grounds
and generate corresponding reasoning chains for decision-making. Through
rejection sampling, we only retain instances where the final answer of
the model matches the ground truth, and balance them so that
yes/no/ambiguous appear in a 1:1:1 ratio and the number of training
instances is equal across languages. These filtered reasoning chains are
used to train $`M`$. Finally, we reapply the two-step prompting
procedure, using the base model for ground selection and the trained
model for theory-guided reasoning.

Table 1: Main results: Macro F1 averaged across languages, grouped by
resource level (High: en, zh, es; Low: ko, hi, ms). Blue and red mark
gains and drops over Base, and bold indicates the best per row per

We evaluate on three target models spanning different sizes and
families: Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma3-4B. Unless a model is
explicitly named, all results and analyses use Qwen3-4B, our default
model, chosen for its multilingual capabilities and inspectable internal
reasoning chains. For evaluation, we use our curated benchmark MCLASH
alongside two additional datasets: MMoralExceptQA ([Farid et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)), a multilingual translation of MoralExceptQA ([Jin et
al., 2022](#bib.bib14)) where the correct decision is always clear-cut
(yes or no), and MoCa ([Nie et al., 2023](#bib.bib10)), an English-only
dataset with ternary labels (yes, no, ambiguous). Together, these
datasets allow us to assess the generalizability of our approach across
multilingual and non-clear-cut moral decision-making scenarios. Both
prompts for ground selection and theory-guided reasoning are presented
in the language of each test instance, and following ([Tam et al.,
2025](#bib.bib79)), the internal reasoning chains are enforced in the
native language using native-language prefill tokens right after the
thinking token \<think\>, equivalent to Okay, such as Primero for
Spanish. This reflects the natural setting in which non-English speakers
will interact with the model, and makes the reasoning process more
transparent to them rather than only the final answer.

Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5 Main Results ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
presents the main results, with the full per-language results for all
models provided in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Full Results and Comparison with MoReBench Dimensions ‣ Appendix C Results ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning"). 1)
Prompting alone is unreliable, but training fixes this. MET improves
over Base on Qwen3-4B (+0.81) but degrades on Qwen3-8B (-0.46) and
Gemma3-4B (-3.46); adding training (MET-D) closes this gap, yielding
consistent gains over Base on all three models (+4.23, +3.02, +0.63). 2)
Our method works on both high- and low-resource languages. Especially on
MCLASH, it helps low-resource languages more, with a consistently larger
gain from MET-D across all three models (e.g., +4.49 vs. +3.50 on
Qwen3-4B, +5.25 vs. +2.36 on Gemma3-4B). 3) Gains generalize across
clear-cut (MMoralExceptQA) and ambiguous (MoCa) datasets. The only
exception is Gemma3-4B on MoCa. After inspecting the model outputs, we
find that MET-D makes Gemma3-4B on MoCa more inclined toward clear-cut
(yes/no) answers, causing a drop in ambiguous F1.

the trained model for both selection and following, (3) and the base
model for ground selection paired with the trained model for
theory-guided reasoning. Comparing (2) and (3), we observe that
replacing the base selector with the trained one performs worse,
indicating that our theory-guided reasoning-focused training does not
transfer positively to ground selection. We therefore use the base model
for ground selection as our default and leave training ground selection
to future work. The comparison between (1) and (3) further shows that
theory-grounded prompting remains beneficial after training,
outperforming direct answering without the grounds.

## 6 Analyses

We examine why our method works and what it reveals about multilingual
moral reasoning. We first verify that ground selection captures relevant
grounds instead of random noise
(§[6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Selection Captures Relevant Grounds ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")),
then show that training increases engagement with the selected grounds
(§[6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Training Increases Utilization of the Selected Grounds ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")).
We also analyze how beneficial grounds differ across languages
(§[6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Beneficial Grounds are Different per Language ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")).
We further show that training improves not only performance but also
legibility, by raising the proportion of native-language reasoning
(§[6.4](#S6.SS4 "6.4 Training Improves Native-Language Reasoning ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")),
and finally analyze cross-lingual transfer
(§[6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5 Cross-Lingual Transfer Reflects Typology ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")).

### 6.1 Selection Captures Relevant Grounds

| Selection | High  | Low   | Avg   |
| --------- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Random    | 66.65 | 55.90 | 61.28 |
| Qwen3-4B  | 67.67 | 57.93 | 62.80 |

Table 3: Effect of ground selection: Model-based selection outperforms
random.

We confirm that ground selection selects relevant grounds rather than
noise along two axes: performance comparison against a random-selection
baseline, and the stability of the selected grounds measured by Cohen’s
$`\kappa`$ across random seeds (within model) and across target models.
As shown in
Table [3](#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 6.1 Selection Captures Relevant Grounds ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning"),
our selection outperforms random selection across both high- and
low-resource languages, with a larger gain in low-resource settings
(+2.03). Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ is 0.468 within model and 0.259 across
models. Considering the inherent ambiguity of the task, the level of
agreement indicates that the selection reflects systematic, non-random
patterns.

### 6.2 Training Increases Utilization of the Selected Grounds

We validate that training leads to improved utilization of selected
grounds in theory-guided reasoning. We sample 20 instances in English,
Chinese, and Hindi and have annotators mark whether each selected ground
is used in the reasoning of Qwen3-4B both before and after training. The
per-instance utilization rate is the fraction of selected grounds used.
Average utilization increases from 52.10% to 61.19% in English, from
31.87% to 37.05% in Chinese, and from 42.00% to 51.75% in Hindi.

However, we note that this metric primarily captures engagement, which
refers to whether the reasoning mentions and applies the given grounds.
This is different from reconciliation, which involves weighing and
integrating these grounds to reach a conclusion. We observe cases where
the number of mentioned grounds increases but reconciliation is absent
(Figure
[18](#A3.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ C.3 Comparison of the Ability of Theory-Guided Reasoning of the Base Model versus the Trained Model ‣ Appendix C Results ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")).
Improving how models reconcile grounds is left to future work.

### 6.3 Beneficial Grounds are Different per Language

For each ground, we filter the instances where the ground is selected in
ground selection and compute the macro-F1 of our trained model on those
instances with and without the grounds included in the prompt for
generating the reasoning chain. The difference between the two F1 scores
quantifies how much each ground contributes to the performance.
Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.3 Beneficial Grounds are Different per Language ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
reports the mean F1 gain per dimension and the top-six beneficial
grounds per language.

Every dimension yields a positive average gain with variance across
languages. Hindi benefits the most broadly, likely because its
low-resource status leaves the base model with weaker structural priors
for Hindi moral reasoning. The Moral Uncertainty dimension shows
cultural friction: it hurts F1 in Korean and Chinese, consistent with
the Confucian emphasis on relational obligations that prescribe a
definite moral stance.

The top-six grounds per language further reveal culturally-grounded
differences. English gains most from Probabilistic Moral Uncertainty
(+9.6), First-principles reasoning (+9.0), and Maximin Reasoning (+4.9),
representing the Enlightenment rationalism of the Anglo-American
discourse, also known as the Analytic Philosophy ([Glock,
2013](#bib.bib80)). Spanish is led by Relation-Based Authority (+11.8),
consistent with the interpersonal interdependency at the core of Latin
familismo ([Lopez et al., 2022](#bib.bib81)). Korean and Chinese both
benefit substantially from Contractarianism, aligning with their
Confucian focus in which obligations are understood as mutually-held
relational contracts.

Together, these results show that beneficial grounds are not
language-agnostic: they track real cultural patterns, underscoring the
importance of considering multilinguality carefully rather than simply
translating English reasoning.

![Refer to caption](2607.11736v1/figures/avg_gain_dim_by_lan.png)

![Refer to caption](2607.11736v1/figures/top6_per_language.png)

Figure 4: Gain per dimension and ground: All dimensions yield positive
gains on average, with language-specific nuances. Hindi benefits most,
likely because the base model has less prior knowledge of moral
reasoning in low-resource languages.

### 6.4 Training Improves Native-Language Reasoning

![Refer to caption](2607.11736v1/figures/ablation_radar.png)

Figure 5: Native-language reasoning: MET-D achieves the highest average
F1 and native-language percentage in reasoning chains, with the only
exceptions being Hindi F1 (a low-resource language) and Chinese F1 and
native percentage (where the base model already reasons natively without
enforcement).

Since native speakers naturally prompt models in their native language
and expect responses in the same language, we fix both the input and
output language to the native language as our default setting. Beyond
input and output, we additionally enforce the internal reasoning chain
to be in the native language, motivated by legibility: end users can
audit the model’s reasoning process only if it is in a language they
understand.

A natural question to pose is whether using native-language reasoning
hurts task performance. To answer this, we use MCLASH to compare four
conditions that share the same input/output language setting but differ
in how the internal reasoning chain is handled: 1) base model (Qwen3-4B)
with no language enforcement on reasoning chains, 2) base model with
explicit prefill tokens to enforce native-language reasoning, 3) our
trained model plus prompting without enforcement, and 4) our full
method, MET-D, with training, prompting, and enforcement. We compare the
performance and the percentage of the native language. We use word-level
language detection for non-Latin languages, where the unicode scripts
uniquely identify the language, and sentence-level language detection
for Latin languages, where per-word detection is unreliable.

Figure [5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.4 Training Improves Native-Language Reasoning ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
reveals a clear pattern, with full numbers presented in
Table [8](#A3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ C.2 Full Numbers for the Native Language Reasoning Experiment ‣ Appendix C Results ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").
Enforcing native-language reasoning via prompting alone hurts
performance on average ($`-2.17`$) as shown in (a). Without training,
the base model lacks genuine multilingual reasoning ability, so forcing
it to reason in a non-dominant language degrades output quality.
Native-language reasoning is thus a trade-off: legibility at the cost of
performance.

Our training breaks the trade-off, improving both performance and
legibility simultaneously. Even without explicit enforcement, the
trained model already reasons predominantly in the native language (from
$`{<}1\%`$ to $`{\approx}90\%`$ across languages) and outperforms the
non-enforced base model by $`+1.23`$ F1 percentage points. Furthermore,
combining training with enforcement yields a gain of $`+2.02`$ points,
demonstrating that MET-D achieves high-quality native-language
reasoning, enhancing both legibility and performance, although some
per-language exceptions emerge: for Hindi, the non-enforced base setting
shows the highest F1, due to Hindi’s low-resource nature; for Chinese,
the same setting shows the highest native-language percentage, as
Qwen3-4B already reasons natively in Chinese without explicit
enforcement.

### 6.5 Cross-Lingual Transfer Reflects Typology

![Refer to caption](2607.11736v1/figures/cross_lingual_f1_heatmap.png)

Figure 6: Cross-lingual transfer: Linguistic similarity improves
transfer. For some high-resource languages (English, Chinese), training
on the language itself hurts performance, while training on a different
language helps.

Even without target-language training, cross-lingual transfer can still
help. We train Qwen3-4B on each language individually and evaluate on
all six
(Figure [6](#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.5 Cross-Lingual Transfer Reflects Typology ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")). 1)
Linguistic similarity drives transfer; cultural similarity does not. The
two SOV languages (Korean and Hindi) each improve the other’s F1 by 2.1
points. SVO Latin-script languages (English, Spanish, Malay) likewise
show positive mutual transfer, while Chinese, though SVO, uses a
different script and breaks this pattern. In contrast, culturally
similar languages Chinese and Korean, both from the Confucian sphere,
show only weak transfer (zh$`\to`$ko $`+0.8`$, ko$`\to`$zh $`-0.4`$). 2)
Training on high-resource languages is not always helpful. For some
high-resource targets (English, Chinese), training on the target
language itself hurts its evaluation while training on a different
language helps. This suggests that single-language training can
reinforce cultural biases in theory-guided reasoning, while multilingual
exposure mitigates them. This is a domain-specific characteristic of
multilingual moral reasoning, since prior findings in other domains
suggest that multilingual mixing typically degrades performance
([Arivazhagan et al., 2019](#bib.bib87); [Blevins et al.,
2024](#bib.bib88)). 3) Korean is a notable outlier. Korean shows an
unusually high own-language gain ($`+9.8`$ points), which we attribute
to its typological isolation: a unique Hangul script and honorific
system, making same-language training the most effective path to
improvement.

## 7 Conclusion

We curate a culturally adapted evaluation dataset and propose a method
that grounds moral reasoning in psychological and philosophical
theories. We carefully curate dimensions and theory-relevant grounds,
then introduce a two-step process consisting of ground selection
followed by theory-guided reasoning. In addition, we present a
self-distillation training strategy designed to improve the ability of
models to adhere to the grounds during reasoning. Our results
demonstrate an average F1 improvement of 3.71 points on MCLASH and 4.23
points on MMoralExceptQA, along with enhanced legibility, reflected in
an increase in native-language usage of 62.13 percentage points. We
further find that beneficial grounds align with the actual
characteristics of each culture, while cross-lingual transfer follows
linguistic typology rather than cultural similarity.

## Limitations

Our approach has two main limitations. First, our training targets
theory-guided reasoning rather than ground selection, so ground
selection still relies on the untrained base model. Second, as discussed
in
§[6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Training Increases Utilization of the Selected Grounds ‣ 6 Analyses ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning"),
how models reconcile multiple selected grounds remains an open question.
Addressing both is a promising direction for future work.

## Appendix A MCLASH Curation

### A.1 Selection of the model for adaptation

We compared two models, Qwen3-32B and GPT-4o ([Hurst et al.,
2024](#bib.bib86)), evaluating their performance in adapting culturally
specific items ([Newmark, 1988](#bib.bib37)) (Figure
[7](#A1.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ A.1 Selection of the model for adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")).
Qwen3-32B demonstrated stronger adaptation abilities, whereas GPT-4o
mainly produced direct translations with limited cultural
considerations. Based on these results, we selected Qwen3-32B for
adapting CLASH multilingually, and subsequently asked human annotators
to review and refine the outputs as needed.

Figure 7: Figure for model selection

### A.2 Details of Adaptation

The prompts used for adaptation, along with the checklist for human
inspectors, are presented in Figures
[8](#A1.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ A.2 Details of Adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
through
[12](#A1.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ A.2 Details of Adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").
We first adapt situations from CLASH using the prompt in Figure
[8](#A1.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ A.2 Details of Adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").
These adapted situations are then presented to human inspectors, who
evaluate and revise them using the checklist in Figure
[10](#A1.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ A.2 Details of Adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
and
[11](#A1.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ A.2 Details of Adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").
After finalizing the situations, we use them to adapt the character
descriptions with the prompt in Figure
[9](#A1.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ A.2 Details of Adaptation ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").
For the character descriptions, we found that Qwen3-32B already performs
well in adaptation, with only minor language issues, such as
occasionally generating text in languages irrelevant to the target
language. Therefore, we corrected these minor issues manually to ensure
linguistic quality, without applying an extensive checklist as was done
for the situations.

Because adaptation revises entities rather than assigning labels,
multiple revision choices may be equally appropriate for a culture. For
example, the U.S. tech company Meta maps to any large Korean tech
company such as Naver or Kakao. With many valid answers, a single
numeric inter-annotator agreement is not well-defined. We instead ensure
the quality with a rigorous inspection checklist and a second pass in
which the authors back-translate each adapted narrative into English to
flag misadapted or unadapted entities, such as a company name that is
still American. We then discussed the flagged cases with the annotators.

### A.3 Dataset Statistics

In this section, we present descriptive statistics for the MCLASH
dataset. Table
[4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.3 Dataset Statistics ‣ Appendix A MCLASH Curation ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
reports the total number of situations and the average number of tokens
for the Situation, Action, and Character Descriptions for each language.
Following the cultural adaptation stages described in Section
[3](#S3 "3 Construction of MCLASH ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning"),
we discard datapoints that contain situations that were irrelevant to
the culture or inadequately adapted by the model during the data
curation pipeline.

Our results exhibit a consistent trend in which culturally adapted
variants yield a higher average number of tokens compared to English,
with increases of up to six times in some cases. This observation aligns
with prior work showing that equivalent content across different
languages may differ in token count by up to $`5\times`$ compared to
that of English due to linguistic and tokenization factors ([Ahia et
al., 2023](#bib.bib85)).

## Appendix B Method

### B.1 Details of Grounds and Prompts

We present the six dimensions and their corresponding grounds below,
with specific prompts for selecting the grounds and their descriptions
presented in Figures
[14](#A2.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ B.1 Details of Grounds and Prompts ‣ Appendix B Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
and
[15](#A2.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ B.1 Details of Grounds and Prompts ‣ Appendix B Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").
We also provide the instructions used to generate responses based on the
selected grounds in Figure
[16](#A2.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ B.1 Details of Grounds and Prompts ‣ Appendix B Method ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning").

Figure 13: Dimensions, grounds, and descriptions: We present six
dimensions, each with a set of specific grounds and descriptions that
the target model can select from.

- •
  Normative Authority: Truth-based Authority ([Railton,
  1986](#bib.bib39)), Reason-Based Authority ([Wood, 2008](#bib.bib40);
  [Reus-Smit and others, 2005](#bib.bib41)), Agreement-Based Authority
  ([Jos, 2006](#bib.bib42); [Brink, 1987](#bib.bib43); [Ashford and
  Mulgan, 2007](#bib.bib44)), Institution-Based Authority ([Zelditch,
  2001](#bib.bib47); [Coleman and Leiter, 2010](#bib.bib48); [Walzer,
  1990](#bib.bib49)), Responsibility-Based Authority ([Macquarrie,
  1972](#bib.bib50)), Relation-Based Authority ([Cobern,
  1993](#bib.bib51); [Cohen, 1988](#bib.bib52)), Human-Nature-Based
  Authority.
- •
  Value Systems: Moral Foundations Theory ([Graham et al.,
  2013](#bib.bib53)), Schwartz’s Value System ([Schwartz,
  2012](#bib.bib54)), Hofstede’s Cultural Dimensions ([Hofstede and
  Bond, 1984](#bib.bib55)), Rokeach’s Value Survey ([Rokeach,
  1967](#bib.bib56))
- •
  Ethical Theories: Deontology ([Alexander and Moore,
  2007](#bib.bib57)), Utilitarianism ([Mill, 2016](#bib.bib58)), Virtue
  Ethics ([Hursthouse, 2017](#bib.bib59)), Care Ethics ([Koggel and
  Orme, 2010](#bib.bib60)), Right-based Ethics ([Raz,
  1984](#bib.bib61)), Contractarianism ([Cudd and Eftekhari,
  2000](#bib.bib62)), Ethical Pluralism ([Ess, 2006](#bib.bib63)),
  Pragmatic Ethics ([LaFollette, 1999](#bib.bib64))
- •
  Cognitive Reasoning Strategies: Step-by-step reasoning ([Wei et al.,
  2022](#bib.bib82)), Harm-benefit analysis, Stakeholder analysis
  ([Freeman, 2010](#bib.bib83)), Counterfactual reasoning ([Fisher,
  2004](#bib.bib84)), Consequentialist framing ([Hendrycks et
  al.,](#bib.bib1) ), First-principles reasoning ([Tovstiga,
  2023](#bib.bib69))
- •
  Conflict Handling Strategies: Context-sensitive resolution ([Dancy,
  2001](#bib.bib65); [Musschenga, 2005](#bib.bib66)), Principle-based
  resolution ([Emanuel, 1995](#bib.bib67); [Phillips,
  2019](#bib.bib68)), Coherence-based resolution ([Daniels,
  1980](#bib.bib70)), Adversarial Testing ([Bench-Capon et al.,
  2009](#bib.bib71)), Perspective-based Resolution, Spectator-based
  Resolution ([Raphael, 2007](#bib.bib72)), Procedural Resolution
  ([Habermas, 2004](#bib.bib73); [Habermas, 1998](#bib.bib74); [Horton,
  2003](#bib.bib75))
- •
  Moral Uncertainty: Monistic Commitment ([Railton, 1986](#bib.bib39)),
  Multi-framework Consideration ([Ess, 2006](#bib.bib63)), Probablistic
  Moral Uncertainty ([MacAskill et al., 2020](#bib.bib77); [Greaves and
  Ord, 2017](#bib.bib78)), Optimization ([Peterson, 2017](#bib.bib76)),
  Maximin Reasoning ([Peterson, 2017](#bib.bib76))

### C.3 Comparison of the Ability of Theory-Guided Reasoning of the Base Model versus the Trained Model

Figure
[18](#A3.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ C.3 Comparison of the Ability of Theory-Guided Reasoning of the Base Model versus the Trained Model ‣ Appendix C Results ‣ MET: Theory-Grounded and Culture-Aware Multilingual Moral Reasoning")
presents examples of the Theory-Guided Reasoning output for the base and
trained models.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 18: Case study without reconciliation on the English instance
854-ama. Among the selected ten grounds, the base substantively engages
with three (Institution-Based, Virtue Ethics, Context-Sensitive); MET-D
engages with eight, adding Right-Based, Contractarianism, Stakeholder,
Harm–Benefit, and Principle-Based. Yet broader engagement does not
translate into reconciliation. MET-D issues a one-line verdict per
framework (“Right-based ethics: … Probably not. Virtue ethics: … so yes.
Contractarianism: … then yes.”), and concludes yes in its internal trace
without explicitly weighing the conflicting verdicts against one
another.
